content:
A later revelation that tells you what an earlier one meant is older than Islam. Scholars call it revelatory exegesis: a new revelation, or a figure who claims one, discloses the true or fuller sense of an older scripture. A Muslim scholar opened a debate on the Islamic dilemma with this idea, and these eight points take his examples one by one and check them against the texts.[1]

The argument itself is answered in The Islamic Dilemma, and the parallel case against the New Testament is set out in the Christian twin of the dilemma. This article stays with method: how each tradition rereads the one before it, and where Islam says the rereading stops. Each entry says how strong it is.

Jeremiah gives Babylon a fixed term. "These nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11), and Jeremiah 29:10 promises a return when the seventy years are done.[2] That reads as a plain number with a plain end, and Babylon fell to Cyrus within a lifetime of the prophecy.

Daniel 9:2 has Daniel reading "the books" and counting the same seventy years. Then Gabriel arrives with a new figure: "Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city" (Daniel 9:24). Read as weeks of years, that is 490 years, and the purpose list in the same verse runs to "seal up vision and prophecy".[3]

So inside the Hebrew Bible a later book takes an earlier prophecy, keeps its number, and moves its meaning on the word of an angel. The earlier text is honoured and reread in the same breath. Strength: firm. The two passages say what is quoted. The figure of 490 rests on reading "weeks" as weeks of years, which is the usual reading and is still a reading.

The Commentary on Habakkuk found in Cave 1 at Qumran (1QpHab) works through the prophet line by line. Each line is quoted and followed by pishro, "its interpretation", which is where the name pesher comes from.

Column 7 does two things. Lines 1 to 5 say God told Habakkuk to write what would come on the last generation "but the completion of the age he did not make known to him", while God made known to the Teacher of Righteousness "all the mysteries of the words of his servants the prophets". Lines 7 and 8 then read Habakkuk 2:3 as meaning "that the last age will be prolonged, and it will go beyond all that the prophets have spoken, for the mysteries of God are wondrous."[4]

The second move is the one to watch. A delay the community had not expected is absorbed by saying the prophets spoke more than they knew. The interpreter, and only the interpreter, holds the key. Strength: firm on what the scroll says. Translations of the Hebrew differ in small wording.

The New Testament does not hide its methods. In Galatians 4:24 Paul says of Sarah and Hagar: "These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar." Two verses on, Hagar "is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and answers to the Jerusalem that exists now".[5] Genesis tells a story about two women and two sons. Paul reads it as a story about two covenants.

He does the same with the wilderness in 1 Corinthians 10. The Israelites "drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ" (10:4), and these things "were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (10:11).[6] Scholars call the second kind of reading typology: an earlier event is a pattern that a later one fills.

Students of early Jewish and Christian interpretation usually name five tools: pesher, midrash (expansion of a text by its gaps and echoes), targum (an Aramaic rendering that paraphrases as it translates), typology and allegory. The labels are modern. The practice is on the page. Strength: firm. Paul uses the word "allegory" himself.

Matthew 2:23 says Joseph settled in Nazareth "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophets: 'He will be called a Nazarene.'"[7] The sentence is in no book of the Hebrew Bible. The suggested sources, and why none of them is a quotation, are checked in Matthew's fulfilled prophecies, checked.

The point for this list is narrower. Matthew presents the line as a fulfilment, and the authority for it sits with the one who reads the prophets, since the prophets themselves do not say it. That is the Qumran move again, carried into a gospel. Strength: firm that the words are absent. What Matthew meant by "the prophets", in the plural, is open.

Most New Testament scholars hold that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, together with a shared source of sayings. This is the two-source view. A minority dispute it, and the entry below holds either way, since the parallels exist whatever the order.

Set the parallels side by side and the editing shows. In Mark 6:5 Jesus "could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people". In Matthew 13:58 he "didn't do many mighty works there because of their unbelief". In the storm, the disciples in Mark 4:38 ask "Teacher, don't you care that we are dying?", and in Matthew 8:25 they cry "Save us, Lord! We are dying!" In Mark 10:35 James and John ask Jesus for the seats beside him. In Matthew 20:20 their mother asks.[8]

Luke says openly that he is working from earlier accounts: "many have undertaken to set in order a narrative", and "it seemed good to me also" to write one "in order" (Luke 1:1–3).[9] A later author takes an earlier sacred account, keeps most of it, and changes what it says about the inability of Jesus, the tone of his disciples and who made a request. Christians receive all three gospels as scripture. Strength: firm on the parallels, which anyone can check. Markan priority is the majority view, and a few scholars hold other solutions.

In 2 Corinthians 3:14–16 Paul says of his fellow Jews: "until this very day at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains, because in Christ it passes away. But to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies on their heart. But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away."[10]

That is a claim about who can read the Torah correctly. The words of Moses stay the same, and their meaning is held to open only to a reader inside the new faith. Once the apostles died, that key passed in practice to the church, which settled which reading of the older books was the right one. The Muslim speaker put it that the church became the authorised interpreter.[1]

A Jewish reader rejects the veil, and with reason: he reads his own book in his own language. The entry takes no side between them and records only that the New Testament itself makes the rereading depend on a later authority. Strength: firm on the verse. The step from Paul to the church as interpreter is a summary of a long history, stated here in one line.

Quran 5:48 says that God sent down the Book "in truth, confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture and as a criterion over it". The word rendered "criterion" is muhaymin.[11]

Al-Ṭabarī glosses it as a witness over the earlier books "that they are truth from God, a trustee over them and a guardian of them", and gives the root sense of haymana as guarding and watching over. He then lists the early readings with their chains. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the reports of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, says "witness" and also that the Quran is a trustee "over every book before it". Several chains through Abū Isḥāq give "entrusted over it". In the report of al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Quran is a witness over the Torah and the Gospel that "judges what came before it of the books". Ibn Jurayj adds a working rule: when the People of the Book tell us something from their book, if it is in the Quran, believe it, and if not, reject it.[12] Ibn Kathir gathers the same glosses.[13]

This differs from pesher in one respect that matters. The Quran rarely quotes a biblical verse and decodes it. It claims the standing of a judge over the content, confirming some, correcting some and leaving the rest. Strength: firm on the verse and the glosses. The glosses come through several chains of mixed quality, and the meaning does not rest on any one of them.

Put the entries in a row and a problem appears. Daniel rereads Jeremiah, Qumran rereads Habakkuk, the gospels reread Mark and the prophets, and the church rereads all of it. If every new claimant may disclose a deeper meaning, no text ever means anything settled. A Christian can put that question to a Muslim, and a Muslim can put it straight back.

The Quran answers it. Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad ﷺ "the Messenger of Allāh and seal of the prophets".[14] Ibn Kathir says of this verse that it "is a text that there is no prophet after him", and that if there is no prophet after him there is no messenger either, and he adds that the hadiths on it are mutawātir, reported by a large number of Companions.[15] The case for finality is set out in Can a later prophet reinterpret the Quran?.

With the seal in place, revelatory exegesis ends at the Quran. Every later reading, the classical tafsīr included, is human work, open to error and to correction by the Arabic text. Strength: firm that Islam claims the stop. Whether the claim is true depends on whether Muhammad ﷺ was a prophet, which this list does not try to prove.

The bottom line

Rereading earlier scripture through a later authority runs through the Bible itself: Daniel on Jeremiah, Qumran on Habakkuk, Paul on Genesis and Exodus, Matthew and Luke on Mark. A critic who calls the Quran false for doing the same has to say why the method is allowed in those books.

The Quran does something narrower and claims something larger. It judges the earlier books as muhaymin, and it closes the series with a final prophet, so its own commentators read it without the right to reread it. That stop is the part of the Islamic claim a reader should test. Allāhu aʿlam.
